borders.before: the lecture introduction, course context, and session learning objectives
borders.after: the biological definition of cancer as a genetic, evolutionary disease requiring a permissive microenvironment
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is standard lecture framing and learning objectives, while subtopic 2 begins substantive teaching on cancer biology.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border earlier is impossible as subtopic 1 is the first subtopic; moving it to subtopic 3 would mix lecture administrative framing with core conceptual definitions.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would conflate opening framing with substantive conceptual content.

borders.before: geographic variations in cancer incidence and the broader debate on genetics versus environment
borders.after: specific infectious agents and pathogens that drive cancer development
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 6 concludes the macro-level epidemiological discussion, whereas subtopic 7 begins the detailed examination of specific environmental causes, starting with pathogens.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 6 is still about general epidemiological geographic patterns, not specific pathogen mechanisms, so the border sits best at subtopic 7.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would merge general etiology and epidemiology with the detailed mechanistic analysis of infectious agents.

borders.before: the detailed mechanism of EBV and malaria co-infection in Burkitt lymphoma
borders.after: dietary carcinogens and fungal aflatoxin leading to DNA adduct formation
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 8 finishes the section on infectious agents, while subtopic 9 shifts to chemical and physical mutagens and their mechanisms of direct DNA damage.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 8 is the conclusion of the pathogen discussion, so moving the border to 8 would strand the Burkitt lymphoma case study with chemical mutagens.
borders.caseForRemoving: Joining the two topics would blur the distinction between pathogen-driven oncogenesis and chemical/physical mutational mechanisms.

borders.before: tissue-specific metabolic activation of carcinogens such as beta-naphthylene in the bladder
borders.after: non-mutagenic carcinogens, asbestos, chronic inflammation, and tumor promotion concepts
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 13 finishes direct/indirect chemical mutagens that form DNA adducts, while subtopic 14 introduces the non-mutagenic promoter concept and inflammation.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 13 is strictly about metabolic xenobiotic activation and DNA adducts, so placing the border before 14 is conceptually precise.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would conflate direct DNA-damaging mutagens (initiators) with non-mutagenic agents that facilitate clonal expansion (promoters).

borders.before: a summary of DNA damage mechanisms, tumor promoters, and host/tissue susceptibility
borders.after: high-throughput whole-genome sequencing and mutational signatures of carcinogens
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 provides a synthesis of biological mechanisms of carcinogenesis, while subtopic 18 starts the lecture's next major question: the experimental and epidemiological methods used to prove carcinogenicity.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 17 summarizes preceding mechanisms, so the new topic naturally begins at subtopic 18 with testing methods.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would merge biological mechanisms of carcinogenesis with methodologies used for carcinogen detection and testing.

borders.before: the Ames test, in vitro assays, and their limitations in recapitulating in vivo biology
borders.after: the concluding lecture summary and societal risk-versus-benefit considerations
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 21 ends the discussion of experimental methods, whereas subtopic 22 delivers concluding takeaways and lecture closing framing.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 21 is entirely focused on in vitro toxicology methods, so the border belongs squarely before the closing remarks in 22.
borders.caseForRemoving: Removing the border would merge the technical methodology section with the final lecture summary and closing remarks.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2 and 3 discuss theoretical definitions and the balance between intrinsic bad luck and environmental factors, whereas subtopic 4 begins listing real-world exposures.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2 through 6 work together to present the broad conceptual framework of cancer etiology, contrasting intrinsic random mutations with environmental exposures through epidemiology and public perception.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 7 lists various oncogenic pathogens broadly, while subtopic 8 focuses exclusively on the history and molecular biology of Burkitt lymphoma.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopic 8 functions as the primary in-depth case study illustrating the general principles of viral/pathogen-driven oncogenesis introduced in subtopic 7.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 9 and 10 cover dietary toxins and UV radiation, while subtopics 11 to 13 focus specifically on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and xenobiotic metabolism.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 9 through 13 all examine physical and chemical mutagens that induce direct DNA damage or adducts via endogenous enzymatic activation.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14 and 15 focus on tumor promotion and inflammation, whereas subtopic 16 examines host developmental timing and susceptibility.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 14 through 17 coherently explore the non-initiating aspects of carcinogenesis, including microenvironmental promotion, chronic inflammation, developmental windows of vulnerability, and a unified mechanistic summary.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 18 and 19 examine human-level evidence (mutational signatures and biobank epidemiology), while subtopics 20 and 21 cover experimental animal and bacterial assays.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18 through 21 systematically address the unified question of how science identifies and proves carcinogenicity across genomic, epidemiological, in vivo, and in vitro models.

topics.label: Lecture Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic introduces the lecturer, the course context, and the core learning outcomes for the lecture.

topics.label: Cancer Etiology: Genetic Factors, Environmental Exposures, and Epidemiology
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics provide a conceptual overview of cancer etiology by exploring intrinsic mutations, environmental risk factors, public perception, and global epidemiological patterns.

topics.label: Infectious Pathogens in Cancer Development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain the roles of oncogenic pathogens and co-infections in driving malignancy, using Burkitt lymphoma as an in-depth case study.

topics.label: Chemical and Physical Mutagens and Mechanisms of DNA Damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail physical and chemical mutagens, their metabolic activation through xenobiotic pathways, and the molecular mechanisms of resulting DNA damage.

topics.label: Tumor Promotion, Host Susceptibility, and Mechanisms of Carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore tumor promoters, chronic inflammation, host developmental windows of vulnerability, and conclude with a synthesis of carcinogenic mechanisms.

topics.label: Methodologies for Assessing Carcinogenicity and Mutational Signatures
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics evaluate the genomic, epidemiological, in vivo animal, and in vitro bacterial testing methods used to establish carcinogenicity.

topics.label: Conclusion and Risk-Benefit Considerations
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic concludes the lecture with core summary points and considerations of daily risk-versus-benefit decisions regarding carcinogen exposure.
